title: What to return
sub: Task, ValueTask and the dangerous async void
cards/0/body:
Task: no result, but you can wait for it. Task<T>: returns a T.

Task is a class: every task is a heap object that the GC later cleans up. ValueTask<T> is a struct with two modes: inside it holds either a ready T value (no heap object) or a reference to a real task (or to a reusable IValueTaskSource) when the result isn't there yet.

It pays off only when the result is often ready right away and the method is called very often. The price is a set of rules: a ValueTask is awaited exactly once, never from two places at the same time, and you don't read .Result before it completes. The reason is the reusable source: it may not support blocking waits, and after completion it may already be serving another operation. Need more? .AsTask() turns it into an ordinary task.
cards/1/title: async void is only for event handlers
cards/1/body:
You can't wait for an async void method: the caller never learns when it has finished.

Exceptions take a different path too. In an async Task method, the exception is stored in the task and is thrown to whoever awaits it. An async void method has no task, so the exception has nowhere to go and is thrown "into the air": in a window, into the UI thread's queue (none of your try blocks catch it there, and by default the app crashes); in a console app or on a server, onto a pool thread, which takes the process down. A try/catch around the call won't help: by the time the exception is thrown, the call has already returned.

Use async void only where an event dictates the signature: button.Click += async (s, e) => …
cards/2/options/0: You can't wait for it, and you can't catch its exception with a try around the call
cards/2/explain: No task means nothing to wait for and nothing to carry the exception.
cards/3/q: A console app: try { SendAsync(); } catch (IOException) { Log(); }, where async void SendAsync() throws IOException after an await. What happens?
cards/3/options/0: The catch doesn't fire: the exception is thrown later on a pool thread and crashes the process
cards/3/options/2: The exception quietly stays inside the SendAsync task
cards/3/explain: SendAsync returned at its first await, so the try is already behind us. async void has no task, so the exception is thrown onto a pool thread, and nobody catches it there.
cards/4/q: Which line is a design mistake?
cards/4/explain: SaveAsync isn't an event handler; it needs async Task so it can be awaited.
cards/5/q: When is ValueTask<T> better than Task<T>?
cards/5/options/0: When the result is often ready right away and the method is called very often
cards/5/options/2: When the method waits a long time for the network
cards/5/explain: The savings are only on the fast path with no waiting. If the method always waits, there is an ordinary task inside anyway, and the difference is negligible.
cards/6/q: What must you not do with a ValueTask? Select all that apply.
cards/6/options/1: Await it from two places at once
cards/6/explain: After completion, the source inside a ValueTask may already belong to another operation. If you need to wait more than once, call .AsTask() and work with an ordinary task.
cards/6/deep: IValueTaskSource is reused to get zero allocations even on the slow path: for example, Socket in .NET keeps one such source for reads and one for writes and hands them out again and again. A repeated await of such a ValueTask will, at best, throw InvalidOperationException (the source checks the operation number, the token); with a source that doesn't check, it gets the result of someone else's operation.
cards/7/pairs/2/1: No allocation if ready right away
cards/8/explain: async Task is a method with no result that can be awaited.
